broad-crested-weir.formula: Q = Cd (2/3)^1.5 sqrt(g) L H^1.5, g = 32.2 ft/s^2; theoretical coefficient (2/3)^1.5 sqrt(g) = 3.0888 (ft units); effective C = Cd x 3.0888, Cd ~ 0.85-0.95. 1 cfs = 448.831 GPM; MGD = GPM x 1440 / 1e6.
broad-crested-weir.edition: First-principles critical-flow open-channel hydraulics - the broad-crested weir discharge - and the USBR Water Measurement Manual (public domain), by name.
broad-crested-weir.freeAccess: Free at usbr.gov/tsc/techreferences/mands/wmm; the critical-flow (2/3)^1.5 sqrt(g) = 3.089 coefficient is a first-principles constant and the user may override Cd with a site calibration.
broad-crested-weir.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
broad-crested-weir.editionNote: The free-flow discharge over a broad-crested weir, the critical-flow member that completes the weir family alongside the sharp-crested V-notch, rectangular, and Cipolletti weirs. A broad, level crest long enough in the flow direction forces the flow through CRITICAL depth on the crest, giving Q = Cd (2/3)^1.5 sqrt(g) L H^1.5, with L the crest width across the channel, H the upstream head above the crest, and g = 32.2 ft/s^2. The theoretical coefficient (2/3)^1.5 sqrt(g) = 3.089 is well below the 3.33 of a sharp-crested (Francis) weir -- a broad crest passes less flow at the same head -- and the discharge coefficient Cd (about 0.85-0.95 for a well-rounded upstream nose) trims it further for boundary-layer and approach losses, so the effective coefficient is about 2.6-2.9. A 10 ft crest at 1 ft of head with Cd 0.90 passes about 27.8 cfs. Broad-crested weirs run spillways, embankment and road-overtopping checks, and long-throated flumes because the rating is stable and the crest tolerates debris and submergence. This is the FREE-flow (modular) rating with critical depth on the crest; heavy downstream submergence reduces it and the approach-velocity head is neglected. An operations aid; the USBR Water Measurement Manual, the weir's calibration, and the operator or engineer of record govern.

assumptions.name: Critical-flow discharge
assumptions.value: Q = Cd (2/3)^1.5 sqrt(g) L H^1.5; theoretical coefficient 3.089 (ft)
assumptions.source: critical-flow hydraulics / USBR Water Measurement Manual

assumptions.name: Discharge coefficient
assumptions.value: Cd ~ 0.85-0.95 (editable); effective coefficient 2.6-2.9, below the 3.33 sharp-crested value

assumptions.name: Free-flow, modular
assumptions.value: critical depth on the crest; heavy submergence reduces it, approach-velocity head neglected

disinfection-ct.formula: CT_achieved (mg-min/L) = chlorine_mg_l * t10_minutes. CT_required for 3-log Giardia is interpolated linearly in chlorine residual (<=0.4 to 3.0 mg/L), temperature (0.5-25 C) and pH (6.0-9.0) over the SWTR free-chlorine table. CT for 4-log virus is interpolated in temperature from the free-chlorine virus table (pH 6-9).
disinfection-ct.edition: USEPA Disinfection Profiling and Benchmarking Technical Guidance Manual EPA 815-R-20-003 (2020), Tables B-1 and B-2, reproducing the SWTR Guidance Manual CT tables (public domain).
disinfection-ct.governance: Estimate. Operator of record and primacy agency govern.
disinfection-ct.editionNote: State primacy agency governs CT compliance; this tile is a planning check, not a compliance report.

assumptions.name: Lookup table
assumptions.value: free-chlorine 3-log Giardia CT, 14 residuals (<=0.4-3.0 mg/L) x 6 temperatures (0.5-25 C) x 7 pH (6.0-9.0)

assumptions.name: t10 contact time
assumptions.value: input is the tracer-derived t10, not the theoretical detention time

assumptions.name: Virus credit
assumptions.value: 4-log virus CT 12 / 8 / 6 / 4 / 3 / 2 at 0.5 / 5 / 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 C, linear in temperature

assumptions.name: Chlorine residual
assumptions.value: residuals below 0.4 mg/L read the <=0.4 row; above 3.0 mg/L the 3.0 row is used with a warning

tank-mix.formula: Acres per tank = tank capacity (gal) / spray volume (GPA). Product per tank = acres per tank x product rate per acre. Tanks needed = ceil(field acres / acres per tank). Total product = field acres x rate. Total carrier water = field acres x GPA.
tank-mix.edition: EPA pesticide label (the label is the law per FIFRA) and NRCS Agronomy Technical Note 5 (spray calibration) by name.
tank-mix.freeAccess: Free at epa.gov/pesticide-labels for label search.
tank-mix.governance: Read and follow the product label. The label is the law (FIFRA).
tank-mix.editionNote: The EPA label governs the rate, carrier volume, re-entry interval (REI), and PPE. Nozzle-output (GPA) calibration is the separate Chemical Application Rate (GPA) tile. Product volume displaces a negligible share of the carrier at label rates. Liquid units in fl oz; dry units in oz (avoirdupois).

assumptions.name: Boom-spray GPA band
assumptions.value: 5-30 GPA typical (flagged outside)

hood-exhaust.formula: Type I: Q = duty_multiplier * L. Wall-canopy duty multipliers (light 200, medium 300, heavy 400, extra-heavy 550 cfm/ft) per IMC 2021 §507.5.1-507.5.4. Single-island canopy (400 / 500 / 600 / 700). Double-island (250 / 300 / 400 / 550). Backshelf / proximity / pass-over (250 / 300 / 400; extra-heavy not allowed). Type II: Q = 100 * L (IMC 507.5.5). Makeup = 0.80 * Q (IMC 508 balance check). Duct area (in^2) = Q / V * 144.
hood-exhaust.edition: IMC 2021 §507.5.1-507.5.4 (Type I) and §507.5.5 (Type II). NFPA 96-2024 governs grease-handling exhaust system design.
hood-exhaust.freeAccess: codes.iccsafe.org for IMC TOC; nfpa.org/freeaccess for NFPA 96 TOC.
hood-exhaust.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed mechanical contractor govern. ACCA Manual J / D / S supersede rules of thumb.
hood-exhaust.editionNote: Duty multipliers are formula coefficients per the published IMC; not a code-table reproduction. AHJ governs final equipment selection.

assumptions.name: Hood-type x duty matrix
assumptions.value: wall-canopy / single-island / double-island / backshelf / proximity / pass-over, each with light / medium / heavy / extra-heavy multipliers

assumptions.name: Type II rate
assumptions.value: 100 cfm per linear foot for Type II hoods over dishwashing appliances; the code sets no rate for other Type II hoods

assumptions.name: Makeup air
assumptions.value: 80% of exhaust as a balance-check rule of thumb; AHJ governs final balance

assumptions.name: Duct velocity range
assumptions.value: Type I grease-duct velocity 500-2000 fpm to keep grease suspended

assumptions.name: Grease-duct slope
assumptions.value: 1/4 in per ft minimum slope back to the hood

hemocytometer.formula: cells/mL = (total_cells / squares_counted) * 10^4 * dilution_factor. viability_pct = (total - dead) / total * 100.
hemocytometer.edition: Standard improved Neubauer hemocytometer; each large corner square = 1 mm x 1 mm x 0.1 mm = 0.1 uL.
hemocytometer.governance: Verify protocol against your lab's SOP before pipetting. A miscalculated dilution can ruin a run or a sample.

assumptions.name: Chamber type
assumptions.value: improved Neubauer (1/10 mm depth)
assumptions.source: convention; older Neubauer / Burker chambers differ

assumptions.name: Counting method
assumptions.value: include cells touching top + left edges, exclude bottom + right (L-rule)
assumptions.source: convention; user is responsible for consistency

burial-depth-300-5.formula: min_cover (in) = Table 300.5 cell for (wiring method, location); cover is measured to the top of the raceway/cable. General earth: direct burial 24, RMC/IMC 6, PVC 18, residential GFCI branch 12, low-voltage 6.
burial-depth-300-5.edition: Minimum cover requirements, 0 to 1000 volts, NEC 2023 Table 300.5, by name.
burial-depth-300-5.freeAccess: NEC is free to read at nfpa.org/freeaccess. Cover is measured to the top of the raceway/cable; the table footnotes (under buildings, in/under concrete, supplemental protection) modify specific cells.
burial-depth-300-5.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
burial-depth-300-5.editionNote: Editions available: bundled values follow NEC 2023. NEC 2026 is the current published edition; jurisdictions on NEC 2017 / 2020 / 2023 / 2026 use slightly different ambient corrections and ampacity ranges; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: Column values
assumptions.value: the <= 1000 V columns: direct burial, RMC/IMC, nonmetallic raceway, residential 120V/20A GFCI branch, and low-voltage irrigation/landscape

assumptions.name: Footnotes
assumptions.value: raceways under buildings (0 in), in/under concrete, and supplemental protection modify specific cells

block-redirect-max-angle.formula: max_direction_change = 2 x asin( block_wll / (2 x line_tension) ), the inverse of resultant = 2 x line_tension x sin(angle / 2); solvable only when WLL < 2 x line_tension, else any turn up to 180 degrees is within rating.
block-redirect-max-angle.edition: ASME B30.26 and standard rigging statics by name; first-principles vector resultant, solved for the angle.
block-redirect-max-angle.freeAccess: The vector-resultant statics are public. The block's rated capacity comes from the manufacturer.
block-redirect-max-angle.governance: Estimate. Head rigger and manufacturer working-load-limit charts govern. Inspect every piece of hardware before the show.
block-redirect-max-angle.editionNote: The largest direction change a block or anchor of a rated WLL can turn a line without the resultant exceeding the rating. The resultant peaks at twice the line tension at a 180-degree turn, so a block rated for at least 2 x line tension handles any redirect; past the max angle, resize the block, the anchor sling, and the attachment point for the resultant. Shock loading multiplies this further - keep margin. The qualified rigger and the block / anchor tags govern.

assumptions.name: Max angle
assumptions.value: 2 x asin( WLL / (2 x line tension) ), capped at 180 degrees when WLL >= 2 x line tension

refrigerant-lineset-charge-adjust.formula: extra_oz = max(0, lineset_length_ft - factory_charge_length_ft) x rate_oz_per_ft; extra_lb = extra_oz / 16.
refrigerant-lineset-charge-adjust.edition: Line-set charge-adder identity by name (extra past the factory pre-charge length, at a per-foot rate); first-principles arithmetic.
refrigerant-lineset-charge-adjust.freeAccess: The linear charge-adder arithmetic is public first-principles; the per-foot rate and factory length come from the equipment nameplate.
refrigerant-lineset-charge-adjust.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
refrigerant-lineset-charge-adjust.editionNote: The per-foot rate and the factory pre-charge length come from the equipment nameplate - they vary by refrigerant and liquid-line size (R-410A on a 3/8 in liquid line runs about 0.6 oz/ft). Only the liquid line adds meaningful charge. Over- or under-charging cuts capacity and drives callbacks; the total is weighed in, not guessed.

assumptions.name: Per-foot rate
assumptions.value: from the nameplate; ~0.6 oz/ft for R-410A on a 3/8 in liquid line

assumptions.name: Factory length
assumptions.value: the factory pre-charge line-set length from the nameplate (~15 ft typical)

punch-capacity.formula: F = capacity_tons x 2000; max thickness = F / (pi x D x shear strength); max round diameter = F / (pi x T x shear strength). The inverse of F = perimeter x thickness x shear strength.
punch-capacity.edition: Punching force as sheared area times shear strength solved for capacity - first-principles as in Machinery's Handbook (Industrial Press), by name; public domain.
punch-capacity.freeAccess: First-principles shear; the shear strength (~0.8 x UTS for mild steel) is user-supplied.
punch-capacity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
punch-capacity.editionNote: The largest round hole (or the thickest material) a press of a given tonnage can punch, the inverse of punch-force: from F = perimeter x thickness x shear strength with a round perimeter pi x D, the max thickness is F / (pi x D x shear) and the max diameter is F / (pi x T x shear), where F is the capacity in pounds (tons x 2000). Keep margin: the press should exceed the punch force, the punch and die need adequate strength, and a shear-ground or stepped punch lowers the peak force. First-principles shear for a round hole; a rectangular or shaped hole uses its own perimeter. A shop aid; the press, tooling, and material govern.

assumptions.name: Round hole
assumptions.value: solves a round hole (perimeter pi x D); a rectangular or shaped hole uses its own perimeter

assumptions.name: Shear strength and margin
assumptions.value: the material shear strength (~0.8 x UTS for mild steel) is user-supplied; keep press and tooling margin

led-tape-max-run.formula: len_max = voltage x sqrt(2 x (tolerance/100) / (power_per_ft x resistance_per_ft)); the inverse of led-tape-run's drop_pct = power_per_ft x resistance_per_ft x length^2 / (2 x voltage^2) x 100.
led-tape-max-run.edition: Constant-voltage LED strip voltage drop solved for the run length, by name.
led-tape-max-run.freeAccess: Standard low-voltage LED-strip loading relation; the strip datasheet governs.
led-tape-max-run.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
led-tape-max-run.editionNote: The longest single end-fed run before the far end dims past the drop tolerance, the inverse of led-tape-run: len_max = voltage x sqrt(2 x (tolerance/100) / (power_per_ft x resistance_per_ft)). A 12 V strip typically walls out around 16-20 ft, a 24 V strip roughly double (the run scales with the voltage); oversizing the PSU does not extend it (power-inject or feed both ends instead); the drop uses the uniform-load approximation (half the full-current drop). A planning aid, not the manufacturer's spec.

assumptions.name: Uniform-load drop
assumptions.value: end-fed uniform load drops half the full-current voltage, so drop scales with length^2 and the max run with the voltage

assumptions.name: Round-trip resistance
assumptions.value: resistance_per_ft must be positive; a zero-resistance strip has no far-end drop to bound the run

hydraulic-drive-flow-limit.formula: gpm = 1714 x drive_hp x efficiency / psi; the inverse of drive_hp = (gpm x psi / 1714) / efficiency.
hydraulic-drive-flow-limit.edition: The fluid-power pump horsepower relation (fluid HP = gpm x psi / 1714) solved for flow, by name.
hydraulic-drive-flow-limit.freeAccess: The gpm-psi-to-horsepower relation and the 1714 constant are standard published fluid-power results.
hydraulic-drive-flow-limit.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
hydraulic-drive-flow-limit.editionNote: The most flow a hydraulic power unit can deliver at a working pressure for a given drive horsepower, the inverse of hydraulic-pump-horsepower: gpm = 1714 x drive_hp x efficiency / psi. Flow trades directly against pressure at a fixed power (more force at the same motor gives up speed), the constant-horsepower curve a horsepower-limiting (torque-limiting) pump control rides (a pressure compensator instead holds a set pressure). The overall efficiency (typically 0.80-0.90 gear/vane, higher for a piston pump) is the fraction of drive power that reaches the fluid. This is the power ceiling; the pump displacement and rpm set the actual flow, so treat it as the maximum the motor can support. A sizing aid; the pump and motor manufacturer's data govern.

assumptions.name: Constant-power trade
assumptions.value: flow varies inversely with pressure at fixed drive power (gpm = 1714 x drive_hp x eff / psi)

assumptions.name: Overall efficiency
assumptions.value: the fraction of drive power reaching the fluid; 0.80-0.90 gear/vane, higher for piston

assumptions.name: Power ceiling
assumptions.value: the delivered flow is set by the pump displacement and rpm; this is the max the motor can support

hydraulic-pump-flow.formula: q_theo = disp x rpm / 231; q_actual = q_theo x vol_eff; q_slip = q_theo - q_actual.
hydraulic-pump-flow.edition: The fluid-power pump displacement-flow relation (theoretical flow = disp x rpm / 231), by name.
hydraulic-pump-flow.freeAccess: The displacement-based flow relation and the 231 in^3/gal constant are standard published fluid-power results.
hydraulic-pump-flow.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
hydraulic-pump-flow.editionNote: Hydraulic pump delivered flow: the theoretical (displaced) flow = displacement x rpm / 231 (231 in^3 per gallon), and the delivered flow = theoretical x volumetric efficiency (typically 0.90-0.95 for gear/vane pumps, higher for piston pumps); the difference is internal slip that grows with pressure and wear. This is the algebraic inverse of the hydraulic-motor speed relation (231 x gpm / displacement x vol_eff), and the delivered gpm is exactly the flow the hydraulic-pump-horsepower tile takes as its input. It does not select the pump, account for the circuit's pressure-drop budget, or size the reservoir/cooling. A sizing aid; the pump manufacturer's data govern.

assumptions.name: Theoretical flow
assumptions.value: disp x rpm / 231 (231 in^3 per gallon)

assumptions.name: Delivered flow
assumptions.value: theoretical x volumetric efficiency; the slip grows with pressure and wear

assumptions.name: Sizing only
assumptions.value: the delivered gpm feeds the pump-horsepower tile; the manufacturer data govern

hydraulic-jack-pressure.formula: jack area = pi x bore squared / 4; working pressure = total load / area; pump flow gpm = area x car speed x 12 / 231; car speed from an installed pump = flow x 231 / (area x 12).
hydraulic-jack-pressure.edition: The jack pressure and flow relations, by name, with ASME A17.1 named as governing relief settings, pressure testing, and the jack requirements not evaluated here. Column buckling over the unsupported length, not pressure, governs a long hydraulic jack.
hydraulic-jack-pressure.freeAccess: Area and flow arithmetic on the user's own jack and pump data; no manufacturer or code table is reproduced.
hydraulic-jack-pressure.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
hydraulic-jack-pressure.editionNote: The two relations are simple and they interact. A larger jack lowers the working pressure -- easier on the cylinder, the packing, and the power unit -- and raises the flow needed for the same car speed, so it wants a bigger pump; a smaller jack does the reverse. That trade is why a jack replacement is not a like-for-like swap unless the bore matches: a different bore changes both the pressure the system runs at and the speed it achieves with the existing pump. The relief valve setting is where the two meet a safety requirement. It must be high enough that the elevator works at full load without lifting the relief, and low enough that it protects the system, and it is set as a defined margin above the actual working pressure, which means it has to be reset if the working pressure changes. A relief left at its old setting after a jack change is either lifting during normal service or no longer protecting anything. Telescopic jacks add a wrinkle worth knowing: the effective area changes as stages extend, so the working pressure is not constant through the travel and the highest pressure occurs on the smallest stage.

assumptions.name: Bore changes three things at once
assumptions.value: working pressure, achieved speed with the existing pump, and the relief setting they were matched to

assumptions.name: Column buckling governs a long jack
assumptions.value: this pressure relation does not touch the governing design case

assumptions.name: Telescopic pressure is not constant
assumptions.value: the effective area changes as stages extend and the highest pressure is on the smallest stage

hoist-rope-safety-factor.formula: rope weight = rope count x length x weight per foot; total suspended load = conveyance + payload + that rope weight; factor of safety = (count x breaking strength) / the total; the depth at which the factor reaches a minimum inverts the same relation.
hoist-rope-safety-factor.edition: The suspended-load factor of safety by name, with the statutory minimum entered because it varies by drum type and rope length (MSHA 30 CFR 57.19021 and 75.1431: winding drum 7.0 - 0.001 L below 3,000 ft and 4.0 at 3,000 ft or more; friction drum 7.0 - 0.0005 L below 4,000 ft and 5.0 beyond; no separate personnel figure), and with the rope retirement criteria named as independent of it. MSHA, the applicable ASME and state hoisting requirements, and the mine's hoisting plan govern.
hoist-rope-safety-factor.freeAccess: Division on the user's own conveyance, rope, and payload data against a minimum they supply; no statutory table is reproduced.
hoist-rope-safety-factor.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
hoist-rope-safety-factor.editionNote: On a shallow shaft the rope's own weight is a footnote; on a deep one it can exceed the payload, and because it hangs from the sheave the whole of it is carried at the top where the factor of safety is checked. A calculation that includes cage and people but not rope produces a comfortable-looking number that is simply wrong, and it is wrong in the UNSAFE direction and by more as the shaft gets deeper. Every rope hangs the full length, so the rope weight carries the rope COUNT as a multiplier, and dropping that count is the same class of error as dropping the rope entirely. Depth, not payload, is what consumes the margin: doubling the shaft on the same cage and the same people takes a substantial bite out of the factor. The second half matters more in practice. A rope with an adequate factor of safety can still be due for retirement, because ropes are retired on CONDITION and on TIME rather than on calculated stress -- broken wires per rope lay, loss of diameter, corrosion, distortion, and in many jurisdictions a maximum service life regardless of condition. A hoist rope that passes this arithmetic and fails the broken-wire count comes out of service, and no factor of safety argument changes that. This is static: it does not model dynamic loads from acceleration, deceleration, emergency braking, or shock, which the statutory factors are partly there to cover, and it does not evaluate friction hoist traction (friction-hoist-traction does), which is a separate and governing check on a Koepe installation.

assumptions.name: The rope count multiplies the rope weight
assumptions.value: every rope hangs the full length; dropping the count is dropping the rope

assumptions.name: Depth consumes the margin, not payload
assumptions.value: the same cage and people at twice the depth is a materially lower factor

assumptions.name: Retirement is on condition and time
assumptions.value: a passing factor of safety does not extend a rope's life by one day

pv-row-shade-angle.formula: profile_angle = atan( L x sin(tilt) / (row_pitch - L x cos(tilt)) ) (the inverse of pitch = L cos(tilt) + L sin(tilt)/tan(profile_angle)); valid when pitch exceeds the footprint L cos(tilt).
pv-row-shade-angle.edition: NREL / Sandia PV array row-spacing geometry solved for the profile angle, by name; the relations are first-principles trigonometry.
pv-row-shade-angle.freeAccess: The row-spacing geometry and the ground-coverage-ratio definition are public NREL / Sandia relations and first-principles trigonometry.
pv-row-shade-angle.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pv-row-shade-angle.editionNote: The inverse of pv-row-spacing: with the pitch fixed by the roof or lot, it returns the lowest solar profile (elevation) angle the layout stays shade-free to -- rows shade each other only when the sun drops below it. Compare it to the winter-design sun elevation at the site (the 9 a.m.-to-3 p.m. solstice altitude from latitude or solar-times): if the shade angle is at or below that, the winter window is clear. Assumes due-south rows and a level field; an azimuth offset or a graded slope is a separate correction.

assumptions.name: Shade angle
assumptions.value: the sun elevation at which adjacent rows just begin to shade; below it the array self-shades

assumptions.name: Pitch constraint
assumptions.value: the pitch must exceed the module footprint L cos(tilt) or the rows overlap

assumptions.name: Assumptions
assumptions.value: due-south rows and a level field; azimuth or slope is a separate correction

dual-fuel-balance-point.formula: gas_per_mmbtu = 10 / afue x rate_therm; hp_per_mmbtu = 293.07 / cop_now x rate_kwh; cop_switch = 293.07 x rate_kwh / gas_per_mmbtu; run_hp = hp_per_mmbtu <= gas_per_mmbtu.
dual-fuel-balance-point.edition: The delivered-Btu fuel-cost comparison (heat-pump $/MMBtu = 293.07 / COP x rate_kwh, gas $/MMBtu = 10 / AFUE x rate_therm, switchover COP where the two are equal), by name; 1 MMBtu = 293.07 kWh and 10 therms per MMBtu are named constants.
dual-fuel-balance-point.freeAccess: The delivered-Btu cost comparison is public arithmetic; dual-fuel setpoint worksheets are widely published.
dual-fuel-balance-point.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
dual-fuel-balance-point.editionNote: The delivered-Btu fuel-cost comparison: heat-pump $/MMBtu = 293.07 / COP x rate_kwh, gas $/MMBtu = 10 / AFUE x rate_therm, and the switchover COP where the two are equal. The switchover COP maps to an outdoor temperature only through the specific unit's COP-vs-temperature curve (from the AHRI ratings or the manufacturer's data, entered separately or read from the cold-capacity tile); the comparison is on operating cost only (it ignores equipment wear, defrost, and comfort); the gas side uses the delivered AFUE. An economic setpoint aid, not a controls-commissioning procedure.

assumptions.name: Delivered cost
assumptions.value: heat-pump $/MMBtu = 293.07 / COP x rate_kwh; gas $/MMBtu = 10 / AFUE x rate_therm

assumptions.name: Switchover COP
assumptions.value: the COP where heat-pump delivered cost equals gas delivered cost

assumptions.name: Mapping to temperature
assumptions.value: the switchover COP maps to an outdoor temperature only through the unit's COP-vs-temperature curve

rotary-phase-converter-sizing.formula: start_demand_hp = start_factor x largest_motor_hp; idler_hp_min = max(start_demand_hp, total_running_hp); start_factor ~2 (normal) or ~3 (high-inertia).
rotary-phase-converter-sizing.edition: Rotary phase converter idler-sizing rule of thumb (industry / converter-manufacturer guidance), by name; NEMA MG-1 across-the-line inrush behavior. The converter manufacturer governs.
rotary-phase-converter-sizing.freeAccess: The sizing rule is a public rule of thumb (the greater of the largest-motor start demand and the aggregate running load); the motors' HP and start character are user-supplied.
rotary-phase-converter-sizing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
rotary-phase-converter-sizing.editionNote: A rotary phase converter (idler plus start capacitors) makes three-phase from single-phase. Its idler must do two jobs: START the largest motor across the line, whose inrush is several times its running current, AND RUN the whole load that operates at once. It is sized on the GREATER of the two: idler HP = max(start factor x largest motor HP, total running HP). A ~2x start factor covers a normal-starting load; a high-inertia or hard-starting load (a big reciprocating compressor, a loaded blade) wants ~3x, and a soft-start or VFD on the large motor lowers it. Undersized, the converter stalls or will not bring the big motor up to speed; oversized, it wastes idle power. A rule-of-thumb screen; the converter manufacturer's sizing data and the motors' actual locked-rotor current govern.

assumptions.name: Two duties
assumptions.value: idler = max(start factor x largest motor, total running load); the greater governs

assumptions.name: Start factor
assumptions.value: ~2x normal, ~3x high-inertia/hard-start; a soft-start/VFD on the big motor lowers it

shaft-torsion.formula: J = pi(d^4 - di^4)/32; tau = T (d/2)/J (= 16T/(pi d^3) solid); theta = T L/(J G).
shaft-torsion.edition: The standard circular-shaft torsion relations (mechanics of materials), by name.
shaft-torsion.freeAccess: The torsion formulas are published free in any mechanics-of-materials reference. The engineer of record governs the design.
shaft-torsion.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
shaft-torsion.editionNote: Circular-shaft torsion: polar moment J = pi(d^4 - di^4)/32, maximum surface shear stress tau = T r / J (= 16T/(pi d^3) for a solid shaft), and the angle of twist theta = T L / (J G). Stress falls with the cube of the diameter and twist with the fourth power. This returns the elastic shear stress and twist for a prismatic circular (solid or hollow) shaft under pure torsion: it does not include a bending or axial load, and does not apply the stress-concentration factor at a keyway, shoulder, or hole (which can multiply the local stress). A design aid, not a substitute for the engineer of record.

assumptions.name: Circular section
assumptions.value: J = pi(d^4 - di^4)/32; tau = T r/J; theta = T L/(J G)

assumptions.name: Pure torsion
assumptions.value: no bending or axial load; elastic and prismatic

assumptions.name: No stress concentration
assumptions.value: keyways, shoulders, and holes raise the local stress; not included

walk-in-cooler-load.formula: transmission = U x area x deltaT; total = (transmission + infiltration + product + internal) x safety; tons = total / 12000.
walk-in-cooler-load.edition: The walk-in cooler/freezer box heat-load method (transmission + infiltration + product + internal, with a safety factor), from ASHRAE Refrigeration, by name.
walk-in-cooler-load.freeAccess: The four-component box-load method is standard published refrigeration practice; the ASHRAE Handbook - Refrigeration covers it.
walk-in-cooler-load.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
walk-in-cooler-load.editionNote: The walk-in cooler/freezer heat load as the sum of four components: the transmission (conduction) load = the panel U-factor x the total envelope area x the ambient-to-box temperature difference; the infiltration (air-change and door) load; the product load (the pull-down and respiration heat, see product-pull-down-load); and the internal load from lights, evaporator-fan motors, and people; the subtotal is multiplied by a safety factor (commonly about 1.10). Thicker insulation (a lower U-factor) reduces the transmission and the compressor directly. The evaporator equipment is selected for a running time: Heatcraft Engineering Manual H-ENGM0408 uses 16 hours for a 35 F room without a defrost timer and 18 hours with one, so the equipment capacity = the box load x 24/16 or 24/18. This sums the entered components; the manufacturer's detailed box-load method and the equipment ratings govern the final selection.

assumptions.name: Four components
assumptions.value: transmission (U A deltaT) + infiltration + product + internal, x safety

assumptions.name: Insulation
assumptions.value: a lower U-factor cuts the transmission and the compressor directly

assumptions.name: Run time
assumptions.value: equipment capacity = box load x 24/16 (35 F room, no defrost timer) or 24/18 (with a timer)

moist-air-enthalpy.formula: h = 0.240 t + W (1061 + 0.444 t) Btu per lb dry air.
moist-air-enthalpy.edition: The I-P moist-air enthalpy relation from the ASHRAE Handbook - Fundamentals, by name.
moist-air-enthalpy.freeAccess: The moist-air enthalpy relation and its sea-level coefficients are standard ASHRAE psychrometric results. A measured chart state and the equipment ratings govern.
moist-air-enthalpy.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
moist-air-enthalpy.editionNote: The I-P moist-air enthalpy h = 0.240 t + W (1061 + 0.444 t) Btu per lb dry air, with t the dry-bulb (F) and W the humidity ratio (lb water / lb dry air): 0.240 is the dry-air specific heat, 1061 the enthalpy of saturated water vapor at 0 F (measured from liquid water at 32 F; dry air is referenced to 0 F), and 0.444 the water-vapor specific heat, all sea-level coefficients. This returns the total heat content of the air at one state: it is the property cooling-coil-total-load differences across a coil and that an economizer control compares, uses the humidity ratio (not RH directly - pair with outdoor-air-mix or a psychrometric chart to get W), and is a design aid, not a substitute for a measured chart state or the equipment ratings.

assumptions.name: Enthalpy relation
assumptions.value: h = 0.240 t + W (1061 + 0.444 t) Btu/lb dry air

assumptions.name: Sea-level coefficients
assumptions.value: 0.240 dry-air cp, 1061 the enthalpy of saturated vapor at 0 F (from liquid water at 32 F), 0.444 vapor cp

assumptions.name: Humidity-ratio input
assumptions.value: W is the moisture input (lb/lb); get it from RH via outdoor-air-mix or a chart

cooling-coil-total-load.formula: Q = 4.5 x CFM x (h_ent - h_lvg) Btu/hr; tons = Q / 12000.
cooling-coil-total-load.edition: The total-heat coil-load relation from the ASHRAE Handbook - Fundamentals, by name.
cooling-coil-total-load.freeAccess: The 4.5 x CFM x enthalpy-difference total-heat relation is a standard airside coil result. The coil rating governs.
cooling-coil-total-load.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
cooling-coil-total-load.editionNote: The total coil load Q = 4.5 x CFM x (h_ent - h_lvg) Btu/hr, where 4.5 = 60 min/hr x 0.075 lb/ft^3 standard air density and the enthalpies come from moist-air-enthalpy; tons = Q / 12000. This captures the full sensible-plus-latent heat the coil removes, unlike the dry-bulb 1.08 x CFM x deltaT which never sees the condensed-moisture (latent) load. A leaving enthalpy above entering returns a negative Q (the coil is heating), not an error. A design aid; the coil selection and equipment ratings govern.

assumptions.name: Total-heat load
assumptions.value: Q = 4.5 x CFM x (h_ent - h_lvg); 4.5 = 60 x 0.075

assumptions.name: Enthalpy source
assumptions.value: entering/leaving enthalpies from moist-air-enthalpy

assumptions.name: Tons conversion
assumptions.value: tons = Q / 12000; negative Q means heating

injector-flow-at-pressure.formula: flow_new = flow_rated x sqrt(dP_new / dP_rated); returnless dP = rail - manifold pressure, return (manifold-referenced) dP = the regulator's base setting; lb/h = cc/min / 10.5.
injector-flow-at-pressure.edition: Orifice flow scaling with the square root of the pressure differential - public physics, no table and no fitted constant. The cc/min to lb/h factor matches the landed injector-size tile (gasoline about 0.72 specific gravity).
injector-flow-at-pressure.freeAccess: The square-root orifice relation is elementary fluid mechanics; injector flow ratings and their test pressure are published on every injector's data sheet.
injector-flow-at-pressure.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
injector-flow-at-pressure.editionNote: Pressure is a WEAK lever because flow follows the square root: it takes four times the differential to double the flow, and no amount of fuel pressure rescues an injector that is simply too small. The differential is where the two fuel systems part, and it is the point of the tile: a RETURN system's manifold-referenced regulator tracks manifold pressure and holds the differential constant, so boost does not change static flow, while a RETURNLESS system holds the RAIL constant, so the differential is rail minus manifold and boost reduces it - a 550 cc/min injector on a 43.5 psi rail flows 19% LESS at 15 psi of boost, losing fuel exactly when the engine wants more. STATIC flow only: this is full-open capacity, not delivered flow at a pulse width, and it says nothing about injector dead time (latency), which shifts with voltage and pressure and must be corrected in the tune. Raising rail pressure also slows opening and can push a small injector out of its linear range at short pulse widths. Ethanol blends change the whole fuel budget. A tuning aid; the injector's flow data and measured fueling govern.

assumptions.name: Square-root orifice law
assumptions.value: flow scales with sqrt of the differential; derived, not fitted

assumptions.name: System type sets the differential
assumptions.value: returnless = rail - manifold; return = constant regulator setting

assumptions.name: Static flow only
assumptions.value: full-open capacity; dead time and pulse-width delivery are not modeled

seismic-vertical-distribution.formula: k = 1 for T <= 0.5 s, 2 for T >= 2.5 s, 1 + (T - 0.5)/2 between; Cvx = wx hx^k / Sum(wi hi^k); Fx = Cvx x V; Vx = Sum Fi for i = x..n (forces at and above the level).
seismic-vertical-distribution.edition: ASCE 7-22 §12.8.3 (Eqs. 12.8-11 and 12.8-12, the vertical distribution and its exponent k) and §12.8.4 (Eq. 12.8-13, the story shear), by name.
seismic-vertical-distribution.freeAccess: The vertical-distribution and story-shear relations are stated in ASCE 7 §12.8.3 / §12.8.4 and reproduced across the public seismic-design literature (FEMA P-1051, the SEAOC design manuals); the arithmetic is public.
seismic-vertical-distribution.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
seismic-vertical-distribution.editionNote: ASCE 7-22 §12.8.3: the equivalent-lateral-force base shear distributes up the height as Fx = Cvx x V (Eq. 12.8-11) with Cvx = wx hx^k / Sum(wi hi^k) (Eq. 12.8-12); the exponent k is 1 for a period at or below 0.5 s, 2 at or above 2.5 s, and linearly interpolated between (the standard also permits taking k = 2 outright in that band as the conservative-for-overturning choice). §12.8.4 (Eq. 12.8-13): the story shear at a level is the sum of the lateral forces at and above it, so the base story carries the full V. The weights are the effective seismic weights per §12.7.2 and the heights are measured from the base; the distribution assumes the ELF procedure is permitted for the structure (the §12.6 system and irregularity limits). A design aid, not a lateral-analysis substitute; the engineer of record governs.

assumptions.name: Distribution
assumptions.value: Fx = Cvx x V with Cvx = wx hx^k / Sum(wi hi^k); a longer period (larger k) shifts force toward the roof

assumptions.name: Exponent k
assumptions.value: 1 at or below T = 0.5 s, 2 at or above 2.5 s, linear interpolation between (k = 2 outright also permitted)

assumptions.name: Story shear
assumptions.value: Vx sums the forces at and above the level (Eq. 12.8-13); the base story carries the full V

insulation-batt-coverage.formula: net = area x (1 + waste%); batts = ceil(net / coverage_per_batt); bags = ceil(net / coverage_per_bag).
insulation-batt-coverage.edition: Batt insulation takeoff from the manufacturer's label coverage per batt and per bag, by name.
insulation-batt-coverage.freeAccess: The area-over-coverage takeoff is public arithmetic; the coverage per batt and per bag come from the manufacturer's label.
insulation-batt-coverage.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
insulation-batt-coverage.editionNote: Batt insulation takeoff: the net cavity area (the wall or ceiling area less the window and door openings) times a waste allowance, divided by the coverage of one batt (a piece) and by the coverage per bag from the product label, each rounded up. The coverage depends on the R-value and the cavity width - an R-13 15 x 93 in batt for 16 in on-center 2x4 framing covers about 9.69 ft^2 (Owens Corning lists 125.94 ft^2 per bag), and a deeper (higher-R) batt is thicker and packs fewer square feet per bag. Insulation is bought by the bag, but counting the batts confirms the wall is fully filled without gaps. This returns the counts; the manufacturer's label coverage for the specific product governs.

assumptions.name: Net area
assumptions.value: cavity area less openings, times the waste allowance

assumptions.name: Counts
assumptions.value: batts = ceil(net / coverage per batt); bags = ceil(net / coverage per bag)

assumptions.name: Label coverage
assumptions.value: coverage per batt/bag from the manufacturer's label

fixed-ladder-fall-protection.formula: a height threshold above which fall protection is required (commonly 24 ft), and rest platforms at an entered interval; a CAGE does not satisfy the fall protection requirement on a ladder installed on or after November 19, 2018; one installed before is accepted until November 18, 2036.
fixed-ladder-fall-protection.edition: Fixed ladder requirements as 29 CFR 1910.28 structures them. The threshold and the rest platform interval are ENTERED because they differ between jurisdictions and have changed; the federal phase-out dates (cages installed before November 19, 2018 acceptable until November 18, 2036, 1910.28(b)(9)) are built in over time.
fixed-ladder-fall-protection.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
fixed-ladder-fall-protection.editionNote: A CAGE IS NOT FALL PROTECTION UNDER THE CURRENT RULE, and that is the finding this exists to surface. Cages were accepted historically and are not accepted on new ladders, because a cage does not ARREST a fall -- it may keep a falling climber roughly within the ladder's plane while they fall the full height inside it. Existing caged ladders are subject to a phase-out, after which a ladder safety system or a personal fall arrest arrangement is required; the cage may remain, it simply does not satisfy the requirement. REST PLATFORMS ARE A DIFFERENT QUESTION and belong to the older provisions -- a ladder with rest platforms and no fall protection is a ladder with no fall protection. The facility-level finding is the useful one: a plant with older fixed ladders almost certainly has several in this condition and a caged ladder reads as a protected ladder to almost everyone who walks past it. A cage on a ladder installed before November 19, 2018 is accepted until November 18, 2036 (29 CFR 1910.28(b)(9)(i)(A), (D)); a cage on a newer ladder, or on a section replaced before then, does not satisfy the requirement now.

assumptions.name: Thresholds are entered
assumptions.value: they differ between jurisdictions and have changed

assumptions.name: Height only
assumptions.value: rung spacing, clearances, climbing space and landing extensions are separate requirements

assumptions.name: Anchorage not evaluated
assumptions.value: a personal fall arrest arrangement needs an adequate one

corroded-pipe-b31g.formula: flow stress = 1.1 x SMYS; A = 0.893 L / sqrt(D t) selects the branch; at A at or below 4.0 the parabolic form P = S_flow (2t/D)[1 - (2/3)(d/t)]/[1 - (2/3)(d/t)/M] with M = sqrt(1 + 0.8 L^2/(D t)), above it the rectangular form P = S_flow (2t/D)(1 - d/t); safe pressure = that divided by the safety factor, but no more than the uncorroded design pressure SMYS x 2t/D / SF; and depth past 80% of wall is unacceptable regardless of length.
corroded-pipe-b31g.edition: The original ASME B31G criterion by name, including the A parameter that selects between its two branches and the 80% screening limit. Acceptance is read against the SAFE pressure, not the predicted failure pressure. It screens a single area of general metal loss on nominal wall: it does not evaluate cracks, gouges, dents, seam or girth weld anomalies, interacting defects, or corrosion under external loading, and it is not a fitness-for-service assessment. Modified B31G and RSTRENG typically permit more on the same defect.
corroded-pipe-b31g.freeAccess: One published criterion evaluated on measured dimensions.
corroded-pipe-b31g.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
corroded-pipe-b31g.editionNote: A corroded area behaves like a blunt flaw whose severity depends on how deep it is relative to the wall AND how long it is relative to the pipe's ability to bulge around it, which is why anomalies are ranked by predicted failure pressure rather than by depth. Two things are easy to get wrong and are therefore computed here. B31G is a TWO-BRANCH criterion and the parabolic form with its bulging factor applies only while A is at or below 4.0; carrying it beyond that overstates remaining strength on exactly the long defects that matter most. And the acceptance is read against the SAFE pressure rather than the failure pressure -- a defect whose failure pressure sits above MAOP can still fail the screen once the safety factor is applied.

assumptions.name: Nominal wall and a single defect
assumptions.value: interacting defects and clusters need a different treatment

assumptions.name: General metal loss only
assumptions.value: cracks, gouges, dents and weld anomalies are outside the criterion

assumptions.name: Conservative by design
assumptions.value: RSTRENG with a river-bottom profile usually permits more

assumptions.name: Safe pressure ceiling
assumptions.value: the safe pressure may not exceed the design pressure of the same pipe uncorroded; the 1.1 flow stress would otherwise let a short, shallow defect read stronger than sound pipe

lfg-flare-capacity.formula: rated capacity = peak flow x (1 + design margin); minimum stable flow = rated / turndown ratio; heat release = methane flow x heating value; credit = methane mass destroyed x its global warming potential.
lfg-flare-capacity.edition: Flare sizing against the manufacturer's rated capacity and turndown. A flare needs roughly 20% methane to hold a flame. The site's gas analysis and the applicable air permit govern.
lfg-flare-capacity.freeAccess: Public arithmetic; the turndown and rated capacity come from the flare manufacturer.
lfg-flare-capacity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
lfg-flare-capacity.editionNote: Flow is not what puts a flare out -- reaching the turndown by decline alone takes decades. Gas QUALITY is: a well field pulled too hard draws air through the cover, dilutes the methane, and trips the flare with plenty of flow still arriving.

assumptions.name: Biogenic carbon dioxide
assumptions.value: the flare's own CO2 is biogenic and is not charged against the credit

assumptions.name: Destruction efficiency
assumptions.value: entered; it is a permit and manufacturer figure, not a calculated one

propane-vaporization-rate.formula: wetted surface of a horizontal cylinder at the entered fill -- the shell arc 2R*acos((R-h)/R)*L plus both head segments -- with the manufacturer's table capacity scaled by the wetted-area ratio and by the temperature-difference ratio.
propane-vaporization-rate.edition: Vaporization capacity from the tank manufacturer's published table, scaled by computed geometry. The rate is NOT derived: it also depends on wind, burial, insulation, paint colour and the duration of the draw.
propane-vaporization-rate.freeAccess: Circular-segment geometry and two ratios on an entered table reading.
propane-vaporization-rate.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
propane-vaporization-rate.editionNote: A propane tank is a boiler, not a container, and BOTH TERMS MOVE THE WRONG WAY TOGETHER in a cold snap: the ambient falls, so the temperature difference driving heat through the shell shrinks, and a drawn-down tank has less wetted surface. That compound is why the failure is a January morning on a tank at 30% and never the full tank in November. The spec says the wetted area 'halves' between 60% and 30% full; it does not -- the shell arc is a chord function of depth, and on the 3.5 by 16 ft tank here the area goes 108 to 76 sq ft, a fall to 70%. The direction is right and the magnitude is not, which is why the area is computed rather than scaled with the fill. FROST IS THE DIAGNOSIS: liquid boiling fast enough to chill the wall below the dew point means the tank is at or past capacity, and the frost then insulates the shell and makes it worse. THE FIX IS NOT A BIGGER REGULATOR -- it is more wetted area, or a vaporizer.

assumptions.name: The table reading is the input
assumptions.value: wind, burial, insulation and paint colour are not modelled

assumptions.name: Horizontal cylinder with flat heads
assumptions.value: a dished or hemispherical head changes the wetted area

assumptions.name: Continuous draw assumed
assumptions.value: intermittent capacity is higher and the table gives both
